The metal stamped parts are assembled through welding at multiple locations and using bolted connections to the entire seatback frame assembly. The aim of this study to perform design optimization on the entire seat back frame to minimize the weight of the seatback for energy-efficiency while satisfying the mechanical performance requirements. Such a design is enabled by the novel additive manufacturing – compression molding process which combines the polymer composites with metal inserts to produce parts with high strength or stiffness-to-weight ratios. In the following, the design optimization of the seatback frame through AM-CM process is entailed below including numerical modeling, topology optimization, subcomponent, and entire seatback frame design. 4.1 Numerical Modeling (Deepak) Design requirements and loading conditions The mechanical performance requirements and the design requirements for the seatback frame are briefly described in this subsection. The entire seat frame along with the platform is shown in Fig. 4.1.1(a). The entire seat frame in its current form is made up of multiple metal components and welded together at multiple locations. The metal seatback frame is shown in Fig. 4.1.1 (b). The design space for the entire seatback is highlighted in Fig. 4.1.1 (c). The designed seatback should be within the design space prescribed here while satisfying the mechanical performance requirements. The seatback will primarily be subjected to two different loading conditions, namely: (a) shoulder weld forces, and (b) shoulder belt force. The shoulder weld forces consist of 6 different forces each acting at a different location in specific directions as shown in Fig. 4.1.2. Each pair of loads represent a moment 10 | P age couple. The peak axial and resultant shear load that the seatback frame would be subjected to are summarized in Fig. 4.1.2 along with their locations. The shoulder belt force corresponds to a single peak load as shown in Fig. 4.1.3. The seatback frame is evaluated for either of these loads and combination of these loads as a reference to begin with. Figure 4.1.1.
